title: BBR Button Board
text: BBR Button Board A button box you build out of tiles. One USB cable to the Driver Station. The Button Board is a modular control panel for FIRST robotics. A main module plugs into the Driver Station laptop over USB and presents itself as a game controller. Everything a driver actually touches lives on tiles — nine-key keypads, single keys, arcade buttons, rotary encoders — daisy-chained off the main module on one four-wire cable. Build the panel you want. Tiles chain in any order. Add one mid-season without rewiring anything. No code on the robot. The board is an ordinary game controller. Your OpMode or robot code reads buttons exactly the way it reads a gamepad. Works with both Driver Stations. An FRC-friendly HID gamepad with 32 buttons, or an XInput gamepad for the FTC Driver Station — one setting, no hardware change. Configured in the browser. Bind a key by pressing it. No firmware rebuild, no config file. LEDs your robot drives. Tiles with RGB keys can be lit from a companion app on the Driver Station laptop, so the panel reacts to what the robot is doing. How it fits together Driver Station laptop │ USB-C ┌────┴──────┐ RS-485, one cable per link │ main ├──── tile ──── tile ──── tile ───┤ │ module │ │ └───────────┘ terminator The main module polls every tile in turn, collects which keys are down, and sends one USB report. From the Driver Station’s point of view there is a single game controller with 32 buttons on it — it never learns that there are tiles at all. Start here If you want to Read Know what the parts are What you have Put a panel together Plugging it together Get buttons working First run Decide which key does what Binding buttons Light the panel from robot state Driver Station app Two things this board deliberately is not: it is not a keyboard, and it does not run your robot code. It is a controller the Driver Station already knows how to talk to, so nothing on the robot has to change to use one.

title: What you have
text: What you have The main module One per panel. It has the USB-C socket, the processor that runs the bus, and two tile connectors. Connects to Driver Station laptop, USB-C Presents itself as A game controller — 32 buttons, 4 axes Drives Up to 31 tiles on one chain Also carries The CFG button, and jumpers for bus termination The main module holds the whole configuration: which key is which button, what colour each LED is, and which USB personality to use. Tiles hold none of it, which is why a tile can be swapped for an identical one without reconfiguring anything. The tiles Every tile is the same on the bus — a small processor, a transceiver, and two connectors — and differs only in what a person touches. Tile What it is Keys mx9 3 × 3 grid of Cherry MX hot-swap keys 9 mx9rgb The same, with an RGB LED under every key 9 mx1 A single MX key 1 arc4 Four arcade buttons, each on a 3-pin JST PH lead 4 enc2 Two rotary encoders with push-to-click shafts 2 encoders + 2 keys Keys on a tile are numbered from 0. Buttons the Driver Station sees are numbered from 1. Those two numbering schemes are separate on purpose — see Binding buttons. Hot-swap means the key switches push in and pull out by hand, with no soldering. A broken switch in the pit is a ten-second repair. The terminators Two per panel, one at each end of the chain, each on a short cable into the spare connector there. They are not tiles: a small 20 mm board with one connector and one resistor on it, and no electronics. The single connector is deliberate — a terminator cannot be cabled through, so it can only ever sit at an end. They matter more than they look. A chain with no terminators still works on a short cable and starts dropping tiles on a long one, which is the kind of fault that only shows up at a competition. Fit both and forget about it — see Plugging it together. What you supply A USB-C cable to the Driver Station laptop. That is the only power the panel needs. Tile cables — one per link in the chain, six-way JST GH, straight through. Key switches and keycaps for the MX tiles, or arcade buttons for arc4. Any Cherry MX-compatible switch fits. What the Driver Station sees Personality Driver Station You get frc FRC (Windows) 32 buttons and 4 axes on one HID gamepad xinput FTC (Driver Hub / phone) An Xbox-360-style gamepad; the 32 buttons map onto its controls This is a setting, not a different board. Change it in the config app, unplug, plug back in. See The config app.

title: Plugging it together
text: Plugging it together The chain Every board — the main module and every tile — has two identical connectors, wired in parallel. Run a cable from one board to the next in any order you like: main module ──── mx9 ──── mx9 ──── enc2 │ │ terminator terminator Order does not matter. The main module finds tiles by asking, not by counting along the cable. Both connectors on a board are the same. There is no “in” and no “out”. Cables are straight through. Pin 1 to pin 1. There is no crossover cable in this system. Up to 31 tiles, and up to about 4 m of cable in total. Terminators go at both ends The two connectors that end up with nothing plugged into them — one on the main module, one on the last tile — each take a terminator. Fit both. A chain missing a terminator usually works on the bench and then loses tiles under vibration or on a longer cable, which reads as a key that “sometimes doesn’t work” rather than as a wiring fault. If your panel is permanently installed and the main module sits at one end of the chain, you can use the main module’s built-in termination jumper instead of a terminator in its spare connector. One or the other, not both. Power The whole panel runs off the USB cable. There is nothing else to plug in. That budget is not unlimited, and LEDs are what spend it. The main module works out the worst-case draw of every tile on the chain and turns the global LED brightness down until the panel fits the budget — so an over-lit panel dims rather than browning out mid-match. If you are running from a port that can supply more than the default, raise the budget in the config app. See LED colours. Adding a tile mid-season Plug it into a spare connector, moving the terminator to the new end of the chain. The main module gives it an address by itself the next time it is powered on. Nothing that was already bound changes. The one thing to know: bindings are stored per tile position, not per physical board. If you swap a faulty tile for an identical one, the replacement inherits the old one’s bindings automatically. If you add a second tile of the same kind, it is a new tile and starts unbound. Binding buttons covers what to do when the board cannot tell which case it is looking at. Cable pinout Six-way JST GH, 1.25 mm pitch. You only need this if you are making cables. Pin Signal 1 GND 2 GND 3 B (−) 4 A (+) 5 5 V 6 5 V Ground and 5 V are doubled to carry the current an illuminated arcade tile can draw. The differential pair sits in the middle, away from the power pins.

title: First run
headings: 3. Check the board sees your tiles
6. Point the Driver Station at it
text: First run Ten minutes, start to finish: plug in, bind a key, watch it register. 1. Plug it in Connect the tiles into a chain, fit the two terminators, and plug the main module into your laptop with a USB-C cable. The power LED comes on immediately. The laptop should find a new game controller by itself — no driver, no install. On Windows, joy.cpl (Start → Run → joy.cpl) shows it and is a useful sanity check throughout. 2. Open the config app Go to the config site in Chrome or Edge and press Connect. The browser shows a list of serial ports; pick the Button Board. Chromium browsers only. The config app talks to the board over Web Serial, which Firefox and Safari do not implement. The page will tell you rather than failing silently. The Connect screen then shows what the board is: firmware version, serial number, how many tiles it can see, and which USB personality is active. 3. Check the board sees your tiles Switch to Diagnose. Every tile in the chain should be listed as online, with the tile kind and how many keys it has. If a tile is missing, work through Troubleshooting — but check the obvious two first: a cable not clicked fully home, and a missing terminator. Press keys. Diagnose shows presses live, straight off the bus, before any binding is involved. This is the fastest way to prove a switch works. 4. Bind a key Go to Configure. The chain is down the left; pick a tile and it is drawn the way it physically is, keys in the right places. Click the key you want to bind. In the inspector, choose the logical button it should be — 1 to 32. Press the key. The board confirms it. That is the whole binding step. Repeat for as many keys as you need. Buttons you never bind simply never press. 5. Save Press Save. Until you do, the configuration lives in RAM and is lost on the next power cycle. Saved configuration survives unplugging, reboots and firmware updates of the tiles. 6. Point the Driver Station at it FRC: the board appears as a 32-button joystick. Assign it a port in the Driver Station the way you would any joystick. FTC: switch the USB personality to xinput on the Connect screen, then unplug and plug back in — the personality only changes at a USB reset. The Driver Hub then sees an Xbox-style gamepad, and Start+A / Start+B binds it as gamepad 1 or 2 as usual. Nothing works and nothing shows up? Hold the CFG button on the main module while you plug the USB cable in. That forces a known-good configuration personality regardless of what is stored, so a board can never be configured into being unreachable. Testing without a robot The Diagnose screen can make the board report button presses that no one is touching — one button at a time walking 1 → 32, one button held, or all of them at once. That lets you prove the Driver Station end of the chain works before any tile is bound, and prove a binding reaches the robot without needing a third hand. Test mode ends by itself when you disconnect, so it cannot be left on by accident.

title: Updating the firmware
text: Updating the firmware Two different things get updated, in two different ways. Both live on the Firmware screen of the config app. Tiles Tiles update over the bus — the same cable they are already plugged into. Nothing is unplugged, no programmer is needed, and one tile updates at a time while the rest of the chain carries on. Open Firmware in the config app. Any tile running older firmware than the images the site carries is listed with an Update button. Press it and wait. Progress is shown as it goes. The tile drops out of the chain for a few seconds and rejoins when it is done. Its address and its bindings are untouched. A tile that loses power partway through an update is not bricked. The updater writes to a staging area and only commits after the whole image has arrived and its checksum matches; a tile that never gets that far comes back on its old firmware. The main module The main module updates over USB, using the same drag-and-drop mechanism as any RP2040 board. Press Update main module in the config app. The board reboots into its bootloader, and the COM port disappears — this is expected, and the config app will tell you it has lost the connection. A USB drive called RPI-RP2 appears on your computer. Drag the .uf2 file onto it. The drive disappears and the board restarts on the new firmware. Your configuration — bindings, LED colours, USB personality — is stored separately from the firmware and survives the update. If the config app cannot reach the board at all, you can get to the same place by hand: unplug the board, hold the BOOTSEL button, plug it back in, and release. RPI-RP2 appears the same way. Which versions am I on? The Connect screen reports the main module’s firmware version, and Diagnose reports each tile’s. Mixed versions across tiles are fine — the board checks that every tile speaks a compatible protocol and flags any that does not, rather than assuming.

title: The config app
text: The config app Everything is configured in a browser. There is nothing to install, and the page talks to the board directly over USB — your configuration never leaves the laptop. Chrome or Edge, on a desktop. The app uses Web Serial, which Firefox and Safari do not implement and which no mobile browser supports. It has to be served over HTTPS or from localhost; opening the files directly with file:// will not work. Press Connect, pick the board from the browser’s port list, and you are in. The board has to be selected by hand the first time — a page cannot go looking for serial ports on its own, which is exactly the protection you want. Four screens Connect Board identity: product, firmware version, serial number, tile count, and whether the stored configuration is valid. This is also where the USB personality is set — frc for the FRC Driver Station, xinput for FTC. The change is stored immediately but only takes effect on the next USB reset, so unplug and plug back in after switching. Configure The panel as it physically is. The chain runs down the left; select a tile and it is drawn in its real layout, so you click the key you mean instead of hunting through a table of numbers. Selecting a key opens the inspector, which does three things: binds it to a logical button, adds it to a group with other keys, and sets its LED colour. See Binding buttons and LED colours. Diagnose What the bus is actually doing. Tiles — every tile the board knows about, its kind, its firmware, whether it is online, and which keys are down right now. Counters — checksum errors and missed replies per tile. Both should sit at zero; a tile that is steadily accumulating either has a cable or termination problem. Power — the LED power budget, the worst-case draw of the current panel, and the brightness that fits it. Test — makes the board report button presses with no tile involved, for checking the Driver Station end on its own. Firmware Updates for the tiles over the bus, and for the main module over USB. See Updating the firmware. Saved versus not saved Changes take effect immediately — bind a key and it works on the next press — but they live in RAM until you press Save. The app shows when there are unsaved changes. That split is deliberate: you can try a layout, decide you preferred the old one, and power-cycle back to it. Without a board The config app runs against a built-in fake board with a few tiles on it, so the interface can be explored, demonstrated or taught with nothing plugged in.

title: Binding buttons
headings: Keys, buttons, and why they are different
What happens when a tile disappears
text: Binding buttons Keys, buttons, and why they are different A key is a physical thing on a tile. Keys are numbered from 0 within their tile, and a key on its own does nothing. A logical button is what the Driver Station sees. There are 32 of them, numbered 1 to 32, and they exist whether or not anything is bound to them. Binding connects the two. Until a key is bound, pressing it registers nowhere. This indirection is the whole point. Your robot code refers to Button 7, and stays true when Button 7 moves to a different key, a different tile, or a different kind of tile entirely. Binding a key In Configure, click the key, choose a button number, and press the key to confirm. The board waits for the press itself, so there is no way to bind the wrong key by mistyping a number. Rebinding a key to a different button replaces the old binding. A key feeds at most one button. Groups: several keys, one button Several keys can feed the same button. The button is pressed while any of them is down. This is what you want for: The same action reachable from two ends of a wide panel. A driver and a co-driver who each need the same override. An arcade button and a keypad key that do the same job. Add a key to an existing button rather than replacing it, and up to 16 keys can share one button. The reverse is not allowed: one key cannot drive two buttons. If it could, releasing it would have to release both, and “which button did that press belong to” stops having an answer. Debounce Mechanical switches make and break contact several times in the few milliseconds around a press. The tile filters that out, and the default — 5 ms — suits every switch these tiles are designed for. You can raise it per tile if a particular switch chatters, at the cost of that much latency on every press. Worn arcade microswitches are the usual reason. What happens when a tile disappears If a tile stops answering — cable pulled, board damaged — every button bound to it reads as released, immediately. Not “stuck at whatever it was last”, which is the failure mode that drives a robot into a wall. Bindings to a missing tile are kept, not deleted, so unplugging a tile to work on the panel and plugging it back in costs you nothing. Swapping and replacing tiles Bindings are stored against a tile’s position on the bus, and the board remembers which physical tile was in each position. Replace a broken tile with an identical one — the new tile takes the old one’s place and its bindings, automatically. Add another tile of the same kind — it is a new tile, and starts unbound. When the board cannot tell those two cases apart, it says so instead of guessing, and the config app offers the choice. Nothing is silently rebound. Saving Bindings work as soon as they are made, but live in RAM until you press Save. Save writes them to flash and reads them back to check.

title: LED colours
headings: Colours follow the button, not the key
text: LED colours Tiles with RGB keys — mx9rgb today — have one addressable LED under every key. There are two independent ways to drive them, and understanding which is which saves a lot of confusion. Two layers Defaults are part of your saved configuration. They are what the panel looks like when it powers up: a red key for the emergency stop, blue for the intake, dark for everything unbound. Set them in the config app’s Configure screen, and press Save. The live layer is set at runtime, over USB, by a companion app on the Driver Station laptop. It is never saved. This is what makes a panel react — flash the arm button red while the arm is out of bounds, light the scoring buttons only when the robot is in range. The live layer wins wherever both are set, per LED. Clearing it returns every LED to the saved defaults. See Driver Station app for how to write to it. Colours follow the button, not the key An LED colour set for a logical button moves with that button. Rebind Button 7 to a different key and its colour goes with it — which is almost always what you meant. LEDs that are not under a bound key — edge glow, spare positions — are addressed by tile and LED number instead. Effects Effect What it does solid On, steady. The default. blink Slow flash fast Fast flash breathe Smooth fade in and out Effects are generated on the tile, so a blink stays smooth no matter how busy the bus is, and a companion app does not have to send anything to keep it going. Press feedback By default a key flashes white while it is held, over whatever colour it was showing. It is a small thing that makes a panel feel like it is working — and on a panel where several keys share a button, it shows which one was actually pressed. You can change the feedback colour, or turn it off per button. Brightness and the power budget The whole panel runs off the USB cable, and LEDs are what spend that budget. Rather than let a big panel brown out, the main module adds up the worst-case draw of every tile on the chain and lowers the global brightness until the total fits the budget. So adding a fourth lit tile dims the panel slightly instead of destabilising it. The Diagnose → Power view shows all three numbers: the budget, the worst case, and the brightness actually in use. If you are running from a port that can supply more than the default, raise the budget there. If a panel cannot fit even at minimum brightness, the board holds the LEDs off and raises a fault rather than trying. The Power view says so. Turning everything off There is a single “all LEDs off” command, and it takes priority over anything else in flight. It is the right thing to reach for when a panel is doing something unexpected on a field.

title: Rotary encoders
text: Rotary encoders The enc2 tile carries two rotary encoders, each with a push-to-click shaft. They are the right control for anything continuous — arm setpoint, shooter speed, LED brightness on the robot — where a button can only step. Encoder tiles are the newest part of the system. The protocol and the config app support them; the tile firmware is still in development. Everything on this page describes the design, not something you can plug in today. What the Driver Station sees FRC. Each encoder can be bound to one of four axes. The axis reports an accumulated position — turn it clockwise and the number goes up, keep turning and it keeps going. Four axes is the whole board, so two enc2 tiles claim all of them. An axis is not a joystick. It does not spring back to centre and it has no deadzone, because there is nothing to return to: the value is where the knob has got to. FTC. XInput’s sticks are sprung and deadzoned, which throws away an accumulated position entirely. So under xinput an encoder becomes pulsed buttons instead: one button pulses per detent clockwise, another per detent anticlockwise, and your OpMode counts them. Pulsed buttons are available under frc too, if you would rather count clicks than read a position. The shaft push The push switch on each encoder is an ordinary key. Bind it like any other key — it takes a logical button number and behaves exactly as a keypad key does. Zeroing An accumulated position needs a defined starting point. The board can zero any axis, or all of them, on command — at the start of a match, or when the mechanism it drives is homed.

title: Install the library
text: Install the library The Button Board can be driven from a program on the Driver Station laptop — reading robot state from NetworkTables and pushing LED colours and display text back to the panel. bb is the Python library for that. You do not need this to use the board. Buttons work through the Driver Station like any gamepad, with nothing installed. This is for making the panel react to the robot. What you need Python 3.9 or newer. pyserial. python3 -m pip install pyserial The library itself lives in tools/bb/ in the repository. Copy that directory next to your script, or put its parent on PYTHONPATH: export PYTHONPATH=/path/to/BBRControlBoard/tools Check it works from bb import Board with Board.open() as board: # finds the COM port by itself print(board.hello()) {'ok': True, 'product': 'Button Board', 'fw': '0.1.0', 'proto': 1, ...} If it cannot find the board, pass the port explicitly — Board.open(port="COM7") on Windows, Board.open(port="/dev/ttyACM0") on Linux. Without a board MockBoard speaks the same protocol in-process, so a companion app can be written and tested with no hardware attached: from bb import MockBoard board = MockBoard() board.led(3, "red") print(board.state.leds) # {('btn', 3): 'led 3 FF0000'} One connection at a time The board’s configuration channel is a serial port, and a serial port has one owner. If the config app has the board open in a browser tab, your script cannot open it, and the other way round. Close one before starting the other.

title: Your first script
text: Your first script A companion app is a loop: read what the robot is doing, decide what the panel should look like, push it. Here is the whole shape of one. from bb import Board with Board.open() as board: leds = board.led_layer() while True: arm_fault = read_from_networktables("arm_fault") in_range = read_from_networktables("in_scoring_range") leds.set(3, "red" if arm_fault else "off") leds.set(7, "green" if in_range else "off", fx="breathe") leds.flush() Why led_layer() and not board.led() Both work. The difference is what happens when nothing changes. board.led(3, "red") sends a command every time you call it. In a 50 Hz loop that is 50 commands a second per button, whether or not the colour changed — the board processes all of them and puts the changes on the bus. led_layer() stages the writes and flush() sends only what changed. A steady panel costs nothing at all. Use it for anything that runs in a loop; use board.led() for one-off changes. leds.set(3, "red") leds.flush() # sends: led 3 FF0000 leds.set(3, "red") leds.flush() # sends nothing Colours Anything sensible works: leds.set(1, "red") # a name leds.set(2, "#0040FF") # hex, with or without the # leds.set(3, (0, 64, 255)) # an (r, g, b) triple leds.set(4, 0x0040FF) # an int leds.set(5, None) # off Named colours include red green blue yellow cyan magenta orange purple pink amber lime teal white off, plus alliance_red and alliance_blue. Effects leds.set(3, "red", "blink") # slow flash leds.set(3, "red", "fast") # fast flash leds.set(3, "red", "breathe") # fade in and out The tile generates the effect, so it keeps running with no further commands. Clearing up board.led_reset() # back to the colours saved in the configuration board.led_all("off") # everything dark, right now led_all("off") is the panic button — it takes priority over anything else in progress. When the board goes away A companion app runs for a whole match, and USB cables get kicked. Every call raises rather than failing quietly: from bb import Board, BoardError try: leds.flush() except BoardError as e: print("lost the panel:", e) # reconnect, then leds.forget() so the next flush redraws everything forget() matters after a reconnect or a reboot: the diffing layer thinks the board still shows what it last sent, and after a power cycle that is no longer true.

title: Python API summary
text: Python API summary Everything here is a method on Board. Each one sends a command and returns the board’s reply as a dictionary, or raises. Connecting Call What it does Board.open(port=None) Open the board, auto-detecting the port board.close() Close it. Also happens on leaving a with block MockBoard() An in-process board, no hardware Identity and state Call Returns board.hello() Product, firmware version, serial, tile count, USB personality board.tiles() A list, one entry per tile: kind, firmware, state, keys currently down board.tile(addr) One tile’s entry, or None board.stats() Uptime, poll cycle time, fault state, LED power budget LEDs Call What it does board.led(btn, colour, fx=None, press=None) Set a logical button’s colour board.led_tile(addr, index, colour, fx=None) Set one LED by tile and position board.led_all(colour) Every LED on every tile board.led_reset() Back to the saved defaults board.led_layer() A diffing writer — see Your first script colour takes a name, "#RRGGBB", "RRGGBB", an (r, g, b) triple, an int, or None for off. fx is "solid", "blink", "fast" or "breathe". press turns the white press-flash on or off for that button. LedLayer Call What it does layer.set(btn, colour, fx, press) Stage a colour layer.set_tile(addr, index, colour, fx) Stage a colour by tile and position layer.flush() Send what changed; returns how many commands went out layer.all(colour) / layer.reset() Send immediately and reset the diff layer.forget() Force the next flush() to resend everything Bindings Call What it does board.bind(btn, add=False) Wait for a key press and bind it. add=True joins a group board.bind_cancel() Stop waiting board.unbind(btn) Remove every key from a button board.unbind(btn, addr, key) Remove one key from a group board.map_get() / board.map_set(m) The whole configuration as a dictionary board.save() Write it to flash bind() blocks until someone presses a key, up to 30 seconds. Encoders Call What it does board.bind_axis(n) Bind axis 1–4 to the next encoder turned board.unbind_axis(n) Remove it board.enc_zero(n=None) Zero one axis, or all of them Display tiles Call What it does board.screen(addr) A row-diffing writer for a display tile screen.text(row, s) / screen.bar(row, col, width, value) Stage a row screen.flush() Send changed rows and commit them together screen.clear() Blank the panel The first display tile is disp1: a 128×32 SSD1306, 21 columns × 4 rows. Take the geometry from screen.cols / screen.rows, which come from the tile’s own descriptor, rather than hard-coding it. No disp1 board has been built yet, so develop against MockBoard(); MockBoard(display=False) reproduces a board older than §14, which answers unknown. The board itself Call What it does board.usb("frc") / board.usb("xinput") Set the USB personality; takes effect at the next reset board.power_budget(mA) Set the LED power budget board.test("walk", 250) / board.test("off") Report button presses with no tile involved board.reset() / board.reset(factory=True) Reboot, optionally erasing the configuration Events The board reports things that happen on its own — a tile lost, a fault raised, a key pressed during binding. def on_tile(ev): print(ev["addr"], ev["state"]) # 3 lost unsubscribe = board.on("tile", on_tile) Names are tile, fault, key, enc, progress and player; "*" receives all of them. Callbacks run on the library’s reader thread. Do not call board methods from inside one — the reader is what completes them, so the call blocks until it times out. Put the event on a queue and handle it in your loop. Errors Exception When CommandError The board refused the command. .err is the reason code Timeout No reply in time NotConnected The port is closed or the cable went away NoBoardFound Auto-detection could not identify a board BoardError Base class for all of the above

title: Serial command reference
text: Serial command reference The board’s configuration channel is a plain text serial port. Anything that can open a COM port can drive it — the config app, the Python library, or PuTTY in the pit with no software installed at all. You send one command per line, ending in a newline. The board answers with one JSON object per line. Every command produces exactly one final line, either {"ok":true,...} or {"ok":false,"err":"..."}. The board may send event lines at any time, marked with "ev". A client has to expect one between its own command and the reply. Baud rate is ignored; any setting works. Enter must send a newline, not a carriage return. PuTTY’s default sends CR, which this channel ignores — so commands appear to be accepted and nothing at all happens. Set it to send LF, or use bbctl. The commands Command What it does hello Identify the board: firmware, serial, tile count, USB personality tiles Every tile the board knows about stats Uptime, poll cycle time, fault state, power budget usb frc | usb xinput Set the USB personality, applied at the next reset bind <btn> Wait for a key press and bind it to that button bind <btn> add Same, but add to the button’s group instead of replacing bind cancel Stop waiting unbind <btn> Remove every key from a button unbind <btn> <addr> <key> Remove one key from a group bind axis <n> Bind axis 1–4 to the next encoder turned unbind axis <n> Remove it enc zero [<n>] Zero one encoder axis, or all of them map get The whole configuration as JSON map set <json> Replace it save Write configuration to flash and verify it led <btn> <rgb> [fx] [press] Live colour for a logical button led tile <addr> <led> <rgb> [fx] Live colour by tile and LED number led all <rgb> Every LED. led all off is the panic button led reset Discard the live layer; back to saved defaults power budget <mA> Set the LED power budget test walk [ms] Press buttons 1→32 in turn, with no tile involved test hold <btn> Hold one button test all Every button at once test off Stop replace <old> <new> Move a tile’s bindings to another address by hand reset Reboot reset factory Erase the configuration and reboot boot Reboot into the USB bootloader for a firmware update rgb is six hex digits or off. fx is solid, blink, fast or breathe. Addresses are 1–31, logical buttons 1–32, keys count from 0. Events Event When tile A tile went online, was lost, was assigned an address, or entered its bootloader fault The fault indicator changed, with the reason key A key was pressed — only while waiting for a binding enc An encoder was turned — only while waiting for a binding progress During a tile firmware update player The FTC Driver Station assigned this board a player number A client that only wants request and response can ignore every line containing "ev". A worked example > hello < {"ok":true,"product":"Button Board","fw":"0.1.0","proto":1,"tiles":3,"mode":"run","usb":"frc"} > bind 7 < {"ev":"key","addr":1,"key":4} < {"ok":true,"btn":7,"addr":1,"key":4,"sources":1} > led 7 FF8800 blink < {"ok":true} > save < {"ok":true,"saved":true} bbctl tools/bbctl.py in the repository is a console for this channel that gets the details right — newline endings, holding the port open so test mode survives, and reading on past event lines to the real reply. python3 tools/bbctl.py # interactive console python3 tools/bbctl.py hello stats # run and exit python3 tools/bbctl.py -p COM7 "test walk 250" # explicit port

title: Troubleshooting
headings: Nothing appears when I plug it in
The config app cannot see the board
A tile is missing from the chain
Buttons stick on, or fire on their own
The Driver Station sees the wrong thing
LEDs are dimmer than I set them
text: Troubleshooting Nothing appears when I plug it in Try a different USB cable. Charge-only cables are common and carry no data. Check the power LED on the main module. Dark means it is not getting power. Hold the CFG button while plugging in. That forces a known-good USB configuration whatever is stored, and is the way back from a board that was configured into being unreachable. If it still does nothing, hold BOOTSEL while plugging in. An RPI-RP2 drive appearing means the hardware is alive and the firmware is the problem — see Updating the firmware. The config app cannot see the board Are you in Chrome or Edge? Firefox and Safari have no Web Serial, and no version of the app will work in them. Is something else holding the port? A serial terminal, another browser tab, or a running Python script will each keep the port to itself. Close it. You must pick the port from the browser’s dialog. The page cannot open one on its own. A tile is missing from the chain In order of how often it turns out to be the cause: A cable not fully clicked home. The commonest fault by a distance. A missing terminator. Both ends of the chain need one. Without them a chain often works on the bench and fails on a longer cable. Two terminators in the wrong places — for example a plug and the main module’s termination jumper at the same end. A damaged cable. Swap it with a known-good one. Check Diagnose → Counters. A tile accumulating checksum errors or missed replies is a wiring or termination problem. A tile that never appears at all is more likely a cable or a dead board. A key does nothing Is it bound? An unbound key registers nowhere. Check Configure. Does the tile see it at all? Diagnose shows presses straight off the bus, before binding. If it shows there and not in the Driver Station, the problem is the binding or the Driver Station. If it does not show there, it is the switch. Hot-swap sockets: pull the switch and look at the pins. A bent pin folds under the switch instead of entering the socket. Buttons stick on, or fire on their own A worn microswitch chattering — raise that tile’s debounce. If every button on a tile misbehaves at once, suspect the bus rather than the switches: check the counters, the cable and the terminators. The Driver Station sees the wrong thing FRC expects frc; FTC expects xinput. Check on the Connect screen. A personality change only takes effect at a USB reset. Unplug and plug back in. Under FTC, bind the pad with Start+A or Start+B as usual. Use Diagnose → Test to settle where the problem is: it makes the board report presses with no tile involved. If the Driver Station sees those, everything from the board to the laptop is fine and the problem is on the bus or in the bindings. LEDs are dimmer than I set them That is the power budget working as intended. The board lowers global brightness until the panel fits the current it can draw from USB. Diagnose → Power shows the budget, the worst case and the brightness in use. Raise the budget if the port genuinely supplies more. If the panel cannot fit even at minimum brightness, the LEDs are held off and a fault is raised — the same view says so. My configuration disappeared It was probably never saved. Changes work immediately but live in RAM until Save is pressed. Unplugging before that discards them. Everything worked yesterday Check firmware versions on Connect and Diagnose. A tile updated to firmware the main module does not understand is reported as incompatible rather than being used — the board tells you instead of behaving strangely.
